newsitem.title: USA: K-III moves to pare debt, refocus, sell some assets.
newsitem.headline: K-III moves to pare debt, refocus, sell some assets.

text.p: Magazine publisher and mass media company K-III Communications Corp. said Tuesday it would restructure, selling non-core businesses such as Daily Racing Form and Pro-Football Weekly, and offer an additional 12.5 million shares of its common stock in a public sale.

The New York-based owner of the Channel One educational television channel and speciality consumer magazines could reap anywhere from $250 million to $350 million from the sale of its non-core assets, analysts said. They said it could raise another $150 million through an offering of its stock, which fell 62.5 cents to close at $12 on the New York Stock Exchange.
K-III will use the proceeds to reduce its roughly $2 billion in debt and outstanding preferred stock, measures analysts said would surely boost the company's current BB- and BA3 credit ratings.

K-II said it would seek to grow in six main areas: workplace learning (Westcott); classroom learning (Channel One and Weekly Reader); speciality consumer magazines (Seventeen, Soap Opera Digest, Truckin', Crafts); technical and trade magazines (Ward's, Telephony); consumer directories (Apartment Guides, World Almanac), and business directories (Pacific Shipper, Bacon's).

To do that, the company said it would sell those businesses it considers non-core. They include Newbridge Book Clubs, New Woman Magazine and Krames Communications, as well as the Katherine Gibbs School, whose sale K-III announced last October.

The company derived about $260 million of its $1.37 billion in revenues from those businesses, or about $24 million in cash flow. But those businesses are in markets that fell below the company's targeted growth rate, K-III said.
Analysts said the moves will make K-III a more tightly focused company and could help it concentrate on growing through small acquisitions to its six newly defined core areas.

"It's some of the best news we've seen come out of K-III in a long time," said Jacob Barker, who follows K-III's bonds for NationsBank. "You'll see a significant inprovement in their credit risk after this."

In a conference call with analysts after Tuesday's announcement, K-III said it expects to achieve a 15 percent overall annual growth rate as a result of the moves. It said half of the growth would come internally, without acquisitions.

Analysts said the company was likely to achieve those estimates. They said that for shareholders, the growth prospects outweigh any negative in the company potentially diluting its stock with more common shares outstanding.

K-III had about 134 million common shares outstanding as of Jan. 30, when it announced its 1996 fourth-quarter and year-end results. After the 12.5 million share offering, slated for April, the company will have just under 150 million shares.
